data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The 'small, independently operated services' premise is often a fiction: in practice, decentralization collapses into a de facto centralization on a small number of shared infrastructure providers (e.g., cloud, DNS, CDNs). Therefore, the comparison is false; the decentralized network inherits the correlated failure modes of the underlying infrastructure while losing the large service's ability to engineer around them.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If small operators were shown to use diverse infrastructure (e.g., different cloud providers, on-premise hardware, different regions) in a way that is uncorrelated, the claim would weaken.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If large services were shown to also depend on the same infrastructure providers (e.g., cloud regions) and to lack the resources or will to build diversity, the claim would weaken.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Decentralization at the application layer does not imply decentralization at the infrastructure layer. Small operators, seeking efficiency, converge on the same low-cost, high-availability infrastructure. This creates a hidden dependency: the network's apparent independence is an artifact of application-layer diversity, but its survival is conditional on the uptime of a small number of infrastructure providers. A large service, by contrast, can afford to build redundant, diverse infrastructure or to pay for diversity; a small operator cannot.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
